verifications.claim: The Mars Climate Orbiter was a $327.6 million NASA probe.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R4: 'a $327.6 million probe'; R1: 'Mars Surveyor '98 program spacecraft development cost 193.1 million dollars. Launch costs ... 91.7 million dollars and mission operations at 42.8 million dollars.' (totals $327.6M)
verifications.reasoning: R4 directly attributes $327.6M to the probe; R1 breakdown for program totals the same amount.

verifications.claim: The Mars Climate Orbiter was launched on December 11, 1998.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'launched ... on 11 December 1998'; R2: 'Launch Dec. 11, 1998'; R3: 'launched on December 11, 1998'; R4: 'launched on December 11, 1998'
verifications.reasoning: Exact date confirmed across all references.

verifications.claim: The Mars Climate Orbiter was to study the Martian climate.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'The two missions were to study the Martian weather, climate, and water ... primary science objectives to: monitor the daily weather and atmospheric conditions'
verifications.reasoning: Directly states study of Martian climate.

verifications.claim: The Mars Climate Orbiter failed on September 23, 1999.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'orbit insertion ... on 23 September 1999'; R2: 'End of Mission Sept. 23, 1999'; R3: 'September 23, 1999'; R4: 'enter orbit on September 23, 1999'
verifications.reasoning: All sources pinpoint failure/loss on this date.

verifications.claim: The Mars Climate Orbiter entered the atmosphere too low and burned up.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'entering the Martian atmosphere at an altitude of 57 km ... destroyed by atmospheric stresses and friction'; R2: 'the spacecraft burned up in Mars' atmosphere'
verifications.reasoning: Direct description of low entry and destruction/burn-up.

verifications.claim: The failure was caused by a navigation error—a failure to convert English units to metric—between teams.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'navigation error resulted from some spacecraft commands being sent in English units instead of being converted to metric'; R3: 'failure to use metric units ... in English units'; R4: 'data mismatch ... imperial units ... expected metric'
verifications.reasoning: All describe unit conversion failure as navigation error cause.

verifications.claim: Lockheed Martin engineered software calculated thruster force in Imperial units (pound-seconds).
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R4: 'Lockheed Martin calculated thruster force in imperial units (pound-seconds)'; R3: 'thruster performance data in English units ... SM_FORCES ... Lockheed Martin Astronautics'
verifications.reasoning: R4 directly attributes to Lockheed; R3 implies via context.

verifications.claim: NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) expected metric (Newton-seconds).
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R4: 'NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) expected metric (Newton-seconds)'; R3: 'data ... required to be in metric units ... trajectory modelers assumed ... metric'; R2: 'onboard software worked in metric'
verifications.reasoning: Directly stated in R4; supported by JPL context in others.

verifications.claim: This caused an in-flight trajectory error.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: R1: 'caused the spacecraft to miss its intended ... altitude'; R3: 'small errors being introduced in the trajectory estimate over the course of the 9-month journey'
verifications.reasoning: Unit error explicitly linked to trajectory error.
